questions.q: Define the medical model of disability in one sentence. What is its primary location of the "problem"?
questions.a: The medical model defines disability as a biological/medical impairment within the individual that needs cure or rehabilitation; the problem is located in the person's body/mind. A wrong answer (e.g., "disability is caused by society's barriers") shows confusion with the social model and inability to recall the model's core individualistic assumption.

questions.q: A teacher says, "We cannot admit a blind child because our school has no Braille books and our teachers aren't trained." Using the social model, explain why this statement reflects a societal failure, not the child's limitation.
questions.a: The social model argues that the child's blindness is an impairment, but the *disability* (exclusion from education) arises because the school lacks Braille materials and trained teachers — these are removable societal barriers. A wrong answer that focuses on the child's blindness as the cause of exclusion reveals a medical-model mindset that naturalizes barriers as inevitable consequences of impairment.

questions.q: Apply both models to this situation: A company refuses to hire a qualified deaf candidate, saying "communication will be too difficult." List two specific barriers from the social-model perspective and two "justifications" the medical model would offer.
questions.a: Social model barriers: (1) absence of sign-language interpreters or assistive tech in interviews/meetings, (2) workplace culture that equates spoken communication with competence. Medical model justifications: (1) the candidate's hearing loss prevents effective communication, (2) accommodating them would require "special" effort beyond normal standards. A wrong answer that merges the two (e.g., "the company is right because deafness causes communication problems") fails to separate impairment from socially created barriers.

questions.q: Analyze the relationship between disability and poverty described in the NCERT text. Why does the social model predict a two-way causal link, while the medical model sees only a one-way link?
questions.a: The social model predicts a cycle: poverty → malnutrition/poor healthcare → higher impairment rates (first link), AND impairment → exclusion from education/employment → deeper poverty (second link). The medical model only sees impairment → poverty (due to individual inability to work) and ignores how poverty creates impairment and how social exclusion deepens poverty. A wrong answer that states "disability causes poverty because disabled people can't work" reflects a purely medical, individualistic causality.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "The Census 2011 expansion from 5 to 8 disability categories was a step toward the social model." Use evidence from the NCERT's description of the Census approach to support your judgment.
questions.a: The statement is partially true but limited. Expanding categories (e.g., adding mental illness, learning disabilities) acknowledges diversity of impairments — a medical-model improvement. However, the Census still counts individuals by impairment type without measuring environmental barriers (inaccessible schools, workplaces, transport), which is the social model's core metric. A strong evaluation notes that counting impairments better is necessary but insufficient for a social-model shift; we need data on participation restrictions. A wrong answer that calls it a full adoption of the social model misses the distinction between counting bodies and measuring barriers.

questions.q: Create a 3-panel comic-strip concept (describe each panel in words) that teaches a Class 8 student the difference between the medical and social models using an Indian school setting. Panel 1: the problem; Panel 2: medical-model "solution"; Panel 3: social-model solution.
questions.a: Panel 1: A girl with crutches stares at a staircase to her classroom; caption: "Priya cannot reach her class." Panel 2: A doctor gives her leg braces; caption: "Medical model: fix Priya's legs so she can climb stairs." Panel 3: A ramp is built; Priya enters with friends; caption: "Social model: fix the staircase so everyone can enter." A poor answer shows only medical interventions (surgery, therapy) in all panels, revealing inability to conceptualize environmental modification as the social-model response.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The medical model of disability views disability as an individual's biological impairment or deficit that requires medical treatment, cure, or ______ to "fix" the person.
Fill in the blank: Imagine a Class 12 student, Rohan, who uses a ______.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can (1) clearly distinguish the medical and social models using their core assumptions, (2) apply both models to a real-life Indian scenario (e.g., inaccessible school, workplace discrimination) and identify which barriers are social vs. biological, and (3) evaluate why the social model is essential for rights-based policies.
